Palestinian Authority calls for international intervention amid West Bank escalation
The Palestinian Authority has warned of the dangers posed by the ongoing Israeli escalation across the occupied West Bank, most recently in Hebron, “where collective punishment measures include the forced displacement of entire neighbourhoods, the demolition of homes and structures, and the closure and siege of Palestinian cities”.
These measures form part of a systematic policy pursued by “the Israeli occupation government” across the occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip, the PA noted in its statement, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Since the beginning of 2025, more than 40,000 citizens have been forcibly displaced from their homes, and displacement continues to this day, the statement said.
The PA said it holds the Israel fully responsible for the escalation and called on the international community to intervene urgently and immediately stop Israel committing further crimes in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The PA said the escalation would bring neither security nor peace to anyone, and that its continuation will only fuel further tension and escalation.

Israeli settlers storm villages near Ramallah, damage Palestinians’ crops
Israeli settlers have stormed the villages of Yabrud and Al Mughayyir, east of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, to forcibly graze their sheep on the agricultural lands of Palestinians and damage their crops, Wafa reports.
The Palestinian news agency quoted local sources reporting that settlers had stormed the villages as part of wider attempts to seize land from Palestinians.

What’s behind Israel’s new military operation in the occupied West Bank?
By 
Stephen Quillen
Israel’s military has launched another major operation in the occupied West Bank, in which it plans to carry out mass arrests, demolish homes, and forcibly displace residents.
The operation follows an attack at an Israeli military checkpoint near Hebron on Friday in which two Israeli soldiers were killed. The two suspected Palestinian gunmen were shot dead.
PM Netanyahu, who ordered a full lockdown of the West Bank, said Israeli forces would go house-to-house in the Hebron neighbourhood that the suspected attackers were from. “We will act to destroy this place, ⁠⁠to change it completely,” he said.
Israeli rights group B’Tselem warned the Israeli government’s planned offensive amounts to “collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.
Read here
 to learn what we know about the Israeli military operation.

Residents of Hebron bracing for the worst
By 
Nour Odeh
Reporting from Birzeit, occupied West Bank
Hebron is sealed off; seven district entrances are closed. Only one or two may allow some pedestrian traffic at times, and it’s extremely unpredictable.
The Hebron municipality has told us that up to half of the neighbourhood attacked overnight by Israeli soldiers in Hebron has been forcibly displaced. At least 200 families are now forced to be outside their homes.
The Israeli army is using a number of homes that they have depopulated as temporary military outposts, raising the Israeli flag there and possibly using them for interrogations later on.
We’re judging by the pattern that we saw in Tulkarem and in Jenin, which is exactly what the Israeli prime minister told us the Israeli army would do.
He said they would use what he described as a successful model in those two cities: Depopulating entire areas, demolishing entire neighbourhoods, and re-engineering the areas; he said the area in Hebron would change permanently after that attack.

Israel believes it’s facing one of its most existential crises in its contemporary history
Zeidon Alkinani, a political analyst, has said Netanyahu’s government is “always promoting the idea of further illegal settlements, and it is not illegal in their eyes”.
“There is a strong consensus among most of the leading parties in the Israeli elections in 2026, and not believing in a Palestinian self-determination to a Palestinian statehood,” Alkinani told Al Jazeera.
He added that Palestine is also an “easy talking point in elections, particularly post October 7, where Israel believes it’s facing one of its most existential crises in its contemporary history – at least, in the political narrative that has been fed by Netanyahu’s government”.
Alkinani argued that despite verdicts by the International Criminal Court, and the positions taken by the United Nations and several European countries, Netanyahu “still enjoys global impunity to conduct political intimidation, kidnapping, and assassinations against anyone who is trying to put international legal mechanisms at the forefront of the solution”.

‘Netanyahu will do everything to hold on power’: Analyst
Abed Abou Shhadeh, a political commentator based in Israel’s Jaffa, has been speaking with Al Jazeera about the upcoming elections in Israel and what it holds for the region at large.
Abou Shhadeh said he “doubts that anything immediate would happen, taken into consideration the security threat that Israel faces, with what’s happening in the region, and what happened in Iran”.
If Netanyahu continues in power, he said, “we’re going to see more radicalisation and extremism both from the Israeli public and the Israeli government”.
Some recent polls, Abou Shhadeh said, show that “the more Israeli society feels under threat, the more they go to the right and adopt more extreme views.” In those polls, Netanyahu’s bloc is currently short of a clear majority.
“Netanyahu might try to initiate something before the election; he has been in power for a long time, and I don’t think he is planning to give that up. He will use everything to keep the same power,” Abou Shhadeh said.
A man on a scooter rides past a billboard featuring Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party in Tel Aviv on October 20, 2026 [AFP]

Saudi-led coalition says two Houthi ballistic missiles headed for Taif and Yanbu intercepted
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition has said air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards the cities of Taif and Yanbu.
Earlier, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence had issued warning alerts for the cities of Jeddah, Taif, Yanbu and Mecca.

Government warplanes reported to have struck Houthi-held Mocha
Yemeni government warplanes have carried out five consecutive air raids on the port city of 
Mocha
, in western Taiz province, a field source has told our colleagues at Al Jazeera Arabic.
The source, who requested anonymity for security reasons, said one raid hit near the city’s port and another struck the ring road. A third hit the coast near the port in the old city, and two more targeted the same stretch of coast.
The source said he saw plumes of smoke rising from the old city and the port area. There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Houthi media reported that government warplanes carried out three strikes on Mocha at dawn on Saturday, before five more hit the city later in the morning.

Israeli military vehicles, bulldozer seen stationed in Hebron’s al-Jalda
Videos posted on Telegram by Palestinians around the al-Jalda area in Hebron city show tense scenes as Israeli soldiers stand guard and military vehicles, shopping trolleys and other objects block the roads.
Israeli forces in the area have also sent in a bulldozer that could be seen alongside other Israeli military vehicles.

Houthis launch attack on Lahij’s al-Maqatra Castle
Fierce fighting has resumed in Yemen between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and the Houthis on the eastern front around Taiz, our colleagues at Al Jazeera Arabic are reporting.
Heavy and medium weapons have been used along with artillery and air strikes.
In Lahij governorate in southern Yemen, the Houthis have also launched an attack on al-Maqatra Castle, a military source told Al Jazeera.
The source said the attack began at 2am (23:00 GMT on Friday) after Houthi military movements and preparations since Friday evening.
The source said the group flew a reconnaissance drone over the castle on Thursday evening and government forces stationed there tried to shoot it down before the attack began at dawn.
Government forces battle against Houthi forces west of the city of Taiz [File: AFP]

Israel elections: Where do the opposing sides differ on their agendas?
Abed Abou Shhadeh, a political commentator based in Israel’s Jaffa, says that since the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza three years ago, the Israeli prime minister has “managed to destabilise not only the region but also the world, especially after the attacks on Iran”.
Before Israel’s elections on Tuesday, he told Al Jazeera there is a difference between the two opposing blocs but that “is not necessarily good for the Palestinians or for the neighbouring countries”.
“Netanyahu and the package come with extremely messianic, dangerous, religious Zionist groups, and their whole discourse is about endless war,” Abou Shhadeh said. “The other side is the Israeli military elite that is represented by Gadi Eisenkot, that sees the limits of power that Israel can use.”
On Palestinian statehood, both sides are on the same page, Abou Shhadeh said, adding, however: “We will see different approaches of occupying the Palestinians.”
Abou Shhadeh said Eisenkot argued that “the Israeli military is extremely overstretched and the demography and geography of the whole space between the river and the sea is not in Israel’s favour”. Meanwhile, “Netanyahu is interested in keeping the status quo and continuing escalation, which apparently helps him with the poll because the Israeli public is extremely radicalised,” Abou Shhadeh added.
Israel’s elections are scheduled for October 27, 2026 [Nir Elias/Reuters]

‘Resolution of economic problems a priority and necessity,’ Iran’s chief justice says
Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei, the head of Iran’s judiciary, has held a series of meetings with economists, stressing that an “immediate resolution of the country’s economic problems is a priority and necessity”.
Mohseni-Ejei said the purpose of the gatherings “is not only to help the government but also to help the country”, Iran’s Mehr News Agency reported.
He added that Iran “must adopt measures and arrangements that, first, resolve the current economic problems and, second, block the grounds and sources of these problems”.
Mohseni-Ejei, right, said the ‘immediate resolution of the country’s economic problems is a priority and necessity’ [File: Handout/Iranian supreme leader’s press office via Anadolu]

Up to 200 families forcibly displaced from their homes in Hebron’s al-Jalda
By 
Nour Odeh
Reporting from Birzeit, occupied West Bank
It was a very tough night for residents of the al-Jalda neighbourhood, where up to 200 families were forcibly displaced from their homes. They carried small bags of clothes with them, but they did not have time to carry any other belongings. The municipality in Hebron has set up temporary shelters for them, but it remains unclear how long this forced displacement will last.
There is a lot of fear that the pledge by the Israeli prime minister to use in Hebron what he described as the successful model employed in the Tulkarem and Jenin refugee camps of forced displacement, could mean months of being away from their homes and possibly losing them to massive demolitions.
Entrances in and out of the district are closed. Some of those roadblocks set up by the Israeli military allow for pedestrian traffic, but movement is extremely difficult, even within the Hebron area.

Yemeni NGO says 21 ‘crimes and violations’ committed by Houthis in 24 hours
The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms claims it has documented 21 crimes and violations committed by the Houthis in Taiz governorate over the past day, according to Yemen’s government news agency, Saba.
The NGO said this included approximately 213 “projectiles” fired at residential areas.
In a report issued today, it said it had documented killings and injuries from shelling and sniper fire, kidnappings, detention in unknown locations, raids on and looting of homes, and attacks on residential neighbourhoods and public roads.

Could Israeli polls end occupation of southern Lebanon?
By 
Justin Salhani
As 
Tuesday’s elections
 in Israel approach, so does the possibility that the government that has overseen the invasion and reoccupation of southern Lebanon could be deposed.
But for people in Lebanon, optimism that a change in the Israeli government would bode well for Israel’s neighbours 
is low
.
“I don’t think anything major – or at all – will change for Lebanon even if there’s a change in [Israeli] leadership,” Beirut resident Fouad Debs told Al Jazeera.
“Any internal change might lead to small, insignificant changes just to show the outside world that Israeli society and politics are not messed up or evil,” the lawyer added.
For many in Lebanon, Israel’s history of airspace violations, ground invasions and occupation has led to a general atmosphere of distrust, regardless of who is in charge of the country.
Read here
 in detail.
A child stands next to the rubble of a building damaged in an Israeli attack in Qennarit in southern Lebanon on June 20, 2026 [Stringer/Reuters]

How much of world’s oil reserves is left amid US-Iran war?
By 
Nils Adler
Far less than before the war began in February, and not all of it can be used.
Aaron Kildow, a senior crude oil analyst at Sparta Commodities, told Al Jazeera that global strategic stocks excluding China and Iran have fallen by nearly 327 million barrels since the end of December with the US, Europe and Japan accounting for about 95 percent of the draw.
He estimated that leaves only about 400 million barrels of usable reserves worldwide, excluding China’s stockpile, which is unlikely to be exported, and Gulf stocks, which could be cut off by a closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Nearly half of these available stocks are in Japan.
Europe has about 76 million barrels uncommitted, but members such as Germany are holding some back for a local emergency, Kildow said.
“Europe is the real wildcard, both on timing and willingness,” Kildow said.
Meanwhile, China’s onshore crude stocks stand at 1.13 billion barrels, down from 1.23 billion in late February but still enough for about 80 days of refinery intake, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
India’s reserves cover just eight days of its imports, the Reuters news agency reported.
Read more 
here
.
Vessels are seen anchored off Bandar Abbas, Iran, along the Strait of Hormuz [File: Amirhossein Khorgooei/ISNA via AFP]
